newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Bonn coalition still talking on tax reforms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bonn coalition still talking on tax reforms.

text.p: German coalition tax experts on Wednesday sought to put the finishing touches on a major tax reform after earlier striking a deal to slash income taxes in 1999.

A tax policy group chaired by Finance Minister Theo Waigel was expected to work until late evening before finalising a tax plan intended to help Chancellor Helmut Kohl win a record fifth general election next year.
Speaking as he entered the marathon final meeting, Waigel said the new income tax rates would create "a real incentive for new jobs" for Germany's unemployment-hit economy.

Waigel did not give details, but sources from the working group said a compromise model had been agreed between Waigel's wish to keep Germany's sliding tax scale and the call by junior coalition partner Free Democrats (FDP) for a low entry rate.

The new tax model would start with a flat 15 percent rate on income between 13,000 ($8,000) and 20,000 marks. The rate would then jump to 22 percent and rise to a top rate of 39 percent on earnings above 80,000 marks.
Income taxes would fall sharply from today's entry rate of 26 percent and top rate of 53 percent.

Government leaders want the lower rates to boost job creation. Unemployment, likely to climb to a post-war record this winter, threatens Germany's efforts to cut state borrowing and qualify this year for European monetary union.

Those jobs fears received fresh impetus in a new government report which predicted an unemployment rate of 11 percent this year. That is equal to 4.2 million jobless, a figure 200,000 higher than the level reflected in Waigel's 1997 budget.
The tax policy group was due to finalise its work by late evening. Coalition parties will meet on Thursday to review the proposals before Waigel announces the reform package (eds: around 1700 GMT).
In addition to the income tax cuts, corporation taxes would fall to 35 percent from 47 percent from the start of 1998.
A slew of tax breaks would also be abolished, but taxpayers would still come out around 24 billion marks better off at the end of the day, coalition sources said.
Waigel said the question of raising the 15 percent rate of value-added tax to help offset the cuts in direct taxation was still open after a coalition meeting on Wednesday morning.

He wants to raise VAT by one point, but a group of regional officials in Kohl's Christian Democrat party (CDU) flatly oppose a hike. Other coalition officials want a bigger VAT rise to help bail out Germany's social security system.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) say they would veto a VAT increase, if used to finance income tax cuts, through their majority in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament. They also said the 13,000 mark tax-free allowance was too low.
"The government should not promise tax cuts on one side and take the money out people's pockets on the other," SPD tax spokesman Joachim Poss told the Boerse Online newspaper.
